newsitem.title: GERMANY: Tietmeyer hopes FX fixing pact to be reached soon.
newsitem.headline: Tietmeyer hopes FX fixing pact to be reached soon.

text.p: A decision could be made as early as September on how final exchange rates will be fixed for Europe's single currency, Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said on Thursday.

"It is necessary for the markets to know in good time how the final exchange rates are fixed," Tietmeyer said in a speech, adding "It is very much my hope that the ministers of finance and central bank governors will arrive at a common opinion on this question at the next informal Ecofin meeting in Luxembourg in September."
The text was prepared for delivery at the first European Equity Traders Convention of the Federation of European Stock Exchanges.

With only 18 months to go before the scheduled launch of currency union, Tietmeyer also said would-be member nations still needed to solve structural problems before entering the union, as the euro could not solve all problems.
"For the euro to be successful, however it is also important for European countries to solve their structural problems and to face up to the new challenges."

He added "the euro cannot pay off past debts nor can it eliminate unemployment that has already been created." "The problems that exist must therefore be solved, if possible, before entry into monetary union," Tietmeyer urged.
Even though the future Euroepean central bank will have the mandate for independence, Tietmeyer said the brand-new institution would still need to earn public confidence.

For example "the confidence markets have always shown in the Bundesbank is based on such experience (that the central bank has been able to defend itself against public pressure)," Tietmeyer said, adding "the European Central Bank still has to earn that confidence, however."

At the same time, Tietmeyer said "if the euro is not given the stability seal of approval by the financial markets and the general public from the outset, the project of monetary union will be standing - economically and politically - on feet of clay."
In order to secure a firmer future for the euro, Tietmeyer listed a number of imperatives but warned most urgently that the fiscal criteria must not be watered down.
"Short-term one-off actions or a relaxation of the Maastricht fiscal criteria would, in my view, give the wrong signals."

Tietmeyer was making only a thinly veiled reference to Bonn's ill-fated plan to revalue Bundesbank gold reserves and use the proceeds to paper over gaping deficit holes. The Bundesbank shot down the idea, calling it creative accounting but has on the other hand signalled willingness to revalue its currency reserves.
Profits from such a revaluation would likely flow to the government next year, and therefore in no way help Bonn's plight to find new funds for its 1997 deficit.
